Note💬 Discussion — Controls Conclusion



The ZymoBIOMICS Microbial Community Standard positive control performed as expected. All eight bacterial genera included in the mock community were successfully recovered.The relative abundances of recovered taxa were broadly consistent with expected composition, although minor deviations were observed, likely reflecting known amplification biases associated with 16S rRNA gene primers.
A small proportion (~1%) of reads were assigned to Enterobacteriaceae without genus-level resolution, likely reflecting limitations of the amplified 16S region or conservative classification thresholds.
Overall, these results confirm the reliability of amplification, sequencing, and taxonomic assignment in the 16S workflow.
We can now remove the controls from the phyloseq object and move on with the ecological interpretation.

saveRDS(ps_16s, "data/ps_16s.rds")




Removal of cholorplast and mitochondria reads
In 16S rRNA metabarcoding datasets, sequences originating from chloroplasts and mitochondria are commonly co-amplified due to the evolutionary origin of these organelles from bacteria. In marine surface waters, such as Greenland fjords, chloroplast-derived 16S sequences from phytoplankton can represent a substantial proportion of total reads, particularly when using universal primers targeting the V4 region (e.g. 515F–806R). While these sequences are biologically meaningful, they do not represent free-living prokaryotic communities, which are typically the focus of bacterial diversity analyses. If retained, chloroplast and mitochondrial reads can dominate sequencing libraries and obscure patterns in heterotrophic and autotrophic bacterial taxa, thereby reducing the resolution and interpretability of microbial community structure.
For this reason, we will remove reads classified as chloroplast or mitochondrial prior to downstream analyses, ensuring that the resulting dataset more accurately reflects the composition and diversity of the target prokaryotic community.
With dada2::assignTaxonomy() using SILVA v138.2, chloroplast and mitochondrial assignments are often found in these places:

Order == “Chloroplast”
Family == “Mitochondria”

The plot shows that chloroplast reads make up a substantial proportion of the dataset in many samples, in some cases approaching or exceeding roughly half of total reads, whereas mitochondrial reads remain consistently low across all samples. The marked variability among samples also suggests differences in phytoplankton biomass or composition across the samples. Chloroplasts are abundant mainly in surface and 15m samples.
These organelle-derived reads are ecologically informative because they reflect the presence of planktonic eukaryotes, particularly phytoplankton, within the sampled communities. However, because this part of the analysis is focused on the prokaryotic community, we will remove the chloroplast and mitochondrial sequences. These reads may nevertheless prove useful later when we will be investigating relationships between planktonic eukaryotes and prokaryotic community structure.

📊 Data visualisation
In this section, we explore the community structure of the RoCSI 16S dataset using the phyloseq object (ps_16s) generated above. We start by visualising read depth per sample, followed by basic taxonomic composition summaries.

Read depth per sample


Code
read_depth <- data.frame(
Sample = sample_names(ps_16s),
Reads = sample_sums(ps_16s),
check.names = FALSE
)

ggplot(read_depth, aes(x = Sample, y = Reads)) +
geom_col() +
theme_minimal() + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number()) +
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) + # Rotate x-axis labels for better readability
scale_x_discrete(
    labels = function(x) substr(x, 1, 6), # Show only the first 5 characters of each label
    breaks = function(x) x[seq(1, length(x), by = 4)] # Show every 4th label
  ) +
labs(
title = "Sequencing depth per sample",
x = "Sample",
y = "Number of non-chimeric reads"
)











Rarefaction curve
Let’s check whether sampling (sequencing) effort was sufficient to capture most of the observed ASV richness.


Code
library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)

otu_tab <- as(otu_table(ps_16s), "matrix")

if (taxa_are_rows(ps_16s)) {
  otu_tab <- t(otu_tab)
}

rarecurve(otu_tab, step = 1000, cex = 0.5, label = FALSE)









The rarefaction curves show that most samples approach an asymptote as sequencing depth increases, indicating that the majority of detectable prokaryotic diversity has been captured.
The sample with 922 ASVs (top curve) is sample 25_St9_D1 The following down with 584 ASVs (2nd top curve) is sample 03_St1_D45

Note💬 Discussion — Beta diversity



The ordination shows clustering of samples by fjord, indicating fjord-level structuring of bacterial communities. Sermilik forms a relatively distinct and tightly clustered group, whereas Tunulliarfik exhibits greater within-fjord variability. Notably, there is considerable overlap between Itterdalk and Tunulliarfik, suggesting partial similarity in community composition and potentially shared environmental controls. Overall, fjord identity contributes to community differentiation, although separation is not absolute among all systems.

library(microbiome)

# 1) Agglomerate to Phylum

# 2) Transform to relative abundance (compositional)

# 3) Top 20 taxa by mean relative abundance (returns taxa_names / OTU IDs)

Note💬 Discussion — Archaeal distributions



Archaeal communities showed a consistent vertical structure across all three fjords, with both Nitrososphaeria and Thermoplasmata largely absent from surface waters and increasing in abundance with depth. This pattern indicates that archaeal activity is concentrated in subsurface and deeper layers rather than in the surface production zone.
Nitrososphaeria (likely Candidatus Nitrosopumilus) exhibited a strong depth-associated increase, particularly at 45 m, consistent with their role as ammonia-oxidizing archaea involved in nitrification. Their distribution suggests that nitrification primarily occurs in deeper, low-light waters where regenerated ammonium becomes available. In Tunulliarfik, their presence at 15 m indicates a shallower nitrification zone compared to the other fjords.
Thermoplasmata (Marine Group II) were generally more abundant and displayed a broader vertical distribution, with pronounced peaks at depth. This pattern is consistent with their role as heterotrophic archaea involved in organic matter degradation. The particularly high abundance observed in Iterdalik suggests enhanced carbon processing in this fjord.
The co-occurrence of both groups at depth across all fjords suggests a tight coupling between carbon remineralization and nitrogen cycling, whereby organic matter degradation by Thermoplasmata could be fueling ammonium production that is subsequently oxidized by Nitrososphaeria.
Actinobacteria
The Actinobacteria are dominated by Micrococcales which are typically aerobic, heterotrophic, and metabolically versatile. They are well known for their ability to utilise a wide range of organic compounds, including relatively low concentrations of dissolved organic matter, and are often considered oligotrophic or stress-tolerant generalists. Many members of this order are also psychrotolerant, allowing them to persist in cold environments, and are capable of coping with environmental stressors such as variable salinity, high turbidity, and oxidative stress. They were more abundant in surface waters of the inner regions of Sermilik and Tunulliarfik fjords, both influenced by marine-terminating glaciers. This pattern is consistent with strong glacier-driven environmental gradients.

Note💬 Discussion — Alpha diversity patterns



Alpha diversity of 18S eukaryotic communities varied among fjords, with Ocean and Tunulliarfik samples generally exhibiting higher richness compared to Sermilik. Shannon and Simpson indices indicate relatively high evenness across most samples, although occasional dominance events were observed (diversity drops), particularly in Sermilik and Tunulliarfik. Compared to 16S prokaryotic diversity, 18S communities displayed greater variability among fjords, suggesting that eukaryotic plankton communities may be more sensitive to local environmental gradients such as stratification and meltwater influence.

  left_join(nodes_df, by = c("from" = "name")) %>% rename(domain_from = domain) %>%
  left_join(nodes_df, by = c("to" = "name")) %>% rename(domain_to   = domain)

# Keep only cross-domain edges
cross_ed <- ed2 %>% filter(domain_from != domain_to)

# Keep only nodes involved in cross-domain edges
cross_nodes <- unique(c(cross_ed$from, cross_ed$to))

graph_cross <- induced_subgraph(graph, vids = cross_nodes)

# Remove isolates just in case
graph_cross <- delete_vertices(graph_cross, degree(graph_cross) == 0)

# Compute degrees in the cross network
deg_cross <- degree(graph_cross)

# Create lookup table
genus_lookup <- deg_tax %>%
  dplyr::select(taxon, Genus_final) %>%
  distinct()

# Convert to dataframe
nodes_df <- data.frame(name = V(graph_cross)$name)

# Join genus info
nodes_df <- nodes_df %>%
  left_join(genus_lookup, by = c("name" = "taxon"))

  geom_node_point(aes(color = domain, size = deg_cross), alpha = 0.9) +

Fjord-specific core subnetworks
To explore whether the cross-domain association network is organized differently among fjords, we can visualise fjord-specific core subnetworks derived from the global 16S–18S cross-domain network. For each fjord, let’s retain taxa present in samples from that fjord, extract the corresponding induced subgraph, and then filter to keep only highly connected nodes (core taxa). This approach provides an exploratory view of the dominant cross-domain network structure within each fjord while avoiding the instability associated with re-inferring sparse networks from small fjord-specific sample sets.

Code
make_fjord_network <- function(fjord_name,
                               graph_obj = NULL,
                               meta_df = NULL,
                               mat16_in = NULL,
                               mat18_in = NULL,
                               degree_threshold = 5,
                               min_taxon_sum = 1) {
  
  if (is.null(graph_obj)) graph_obj <- graph_cross
  if (is.null(meta_df)) meta_df <- meta
  if (is.null(mat16_in)) mat16_in <- mat16
  if (is.null(mat18_in)) mat18_in <- mat18
  
  # Samples from that fjord
  samp <- meta_df$Sample[meta_df$Fjord == fjord_name]
  
  # Taxa present in that fjord
  bac_present <- rownames(mat16_in)[rowSums(mat16_in[, samp, drop = FALSE]) >= min_taxon_sum]
  euk_present <- rownames(mat18_in)[rowSums(mat18_in[, samp, drop = FALSE]) >= min_taxon_sum]
  taxa_present <- unique(c(bac_present, euk_present))
  
  # Keep only taxa that are also in the global cross-domain graph
  taxa_present <- intersect(taxa_present, V(graph_obj)$name)
  
  # Induced fjord subgraph
  g_fjord <- induced_subgraph(graph_obj, vids = taxa_present)
  
  # Remove isolated nodes
  g_fjord <- delete_vertices(g_fjord, degree(g_fjord) == 0)
  
  if (vcount(g_fjord) == 0) return(NULL)
  
  # Core filtering by degree within fjord subgraph
  deg_fjord <- degree(g_fjord)
  keep_nodes <- names(deg_fjord[deg_fjord > degree_threshold])
  
  g_core <- induced_subgraph(g_fjord, vids = keep_nodes)
  g_core <- delete_vertices(g_core, degree(g_core) == 0)
  
  if (vcount(g_core) == 0) return(NULL)
  
  # Build nodes table
  nodes <- data.frame(
    id    = V(g_core)$name,
    label = ifelse(!is.na(V(g_core)$genus_clean),
                   V(g_core)$genus_clean,
                   V(g_core)$name),
    group = V(g_core)$domain,
    value = degree(g_core),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  
  nodes$color <- ifelse(nodes$group == "Bacteria", "#2C7FB8", "#D95F0E")
  
  # Build edge table
  edges <- as_data_frame(g_core, what = "edges") %>%
    transmute(from = from, to = to)
  
  visNetwork(nodes, edges, height = "750px", width = "100%") %>%
    visNodes(borderWidth = 1) %>%
    visOptions(
      highlightNearest = TRUE,
      nodesIdSelection = TRUE
    ) %>%
    visInteraction(
      navigationButtons = TRUE,
      zoomView = TRUE,
      dragNodes = TRUE,
      dragView = TRUE
    ) %>%
    visPhysics(stabilization = TRUE) %>%
    visLayout(randomSeed = 7) %>%
    visLegend()
}

PICRUSt2 is giving you three levels of functional prediction from your 16S data:

KO = KEGG Ortholog
EC = Enzyme Commission number
Pathway = usually MetaCyc pathway in PICRUSt2 by default

They are related, but they are not the same kind of annotation. PICRUSt2 predicts gene-family abundances such as KO and EC, and then uses EC-based mappings to infer higher-level pathway abundances/coverage.
